findings.content: Off-by-one bug: changed `>=` to `>` makes the upper bound incorrect. Valid indices for `items` are `0 .. size()-1`. Using `>` permits access at `index == items.size()`, which is out-of-bounds and causes undefined behavior when `*items[index]` is dereferenced. Revert to `>=`.

Raw pointer used to track a member owned by `std::unique_ptr`. This violates the smart pointer / RAII guidelines and introduces a dangling-pointer hazard: any subsequent `push_back` that triggers vector reallocation will invalidate `first_item`. Either drop the cached pointer, hold an index (`std::optional<std::size_t>`), or update `first_item` after every mutation under a single owner.

Off-by-one in bounds check: changing `>=` to `>` allows `index == items.size()`, which then dereferences `items[items.size()]` — out-of-bounds access. Valid indices are `[0, items.size())`, so the original `>=` was correct.

Lifetime hazard: `first_item` is a raw pointer into memory owned by `items[0]`'s `unique_ptr`. It is set only on the first `append` (to `items.front().get()`), so any subsequent reallocation of the `std::vector` invalidates it, and any operation that removes or replaces the first element (e.g. `erase`, `pop_back` on the only element, `clear`, `~Items`) leaves it dangling. Either drop the member, store an index/size_t, or use an observer/weak reference and update it whenever `items[0]` may be reallocated or destroyed.

`first_item` is added but never read anywhere in the codebase; it only acts as a write-only cache of `items.front().get()`. This is dead state and a maintenance trap (see lifetime hazard above). Remove it or wire it to actual call sites.

Off-by-one in bounds allows `index == items.size()`, which is out-of-bounds for `items[index]` (valid range is `0..size()-1`). The original `>=` was correct; the new `>` permits undefined behavior on the boundary.
